description:
What Would You See if Two Galaxies Collided?

Episode 115 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌌
We watch galaxies collide: why the stars almost never hit each other, the Antennae and Mice galaxies, bursts of new star birth, merging black holes, and how the Milky Way itself is built from galaxies it swallowed.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 116: Next stop, the Magellanic Clouds. Two galaxies you can see with your own eyes.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #galaxies #astronomy #shorts #science #nasa

segments.text: What would you see if two galaxies collided? Almost nothing would hit you.
Galaxies crash into each other all the time. It's how they grow.
segments.headline: Galaxies collide

segments.text: But the stars almost never hit each other. The space between stars is enormous.
If the Sun were a grain of sand, the next star would be another grain about thirty kilometers away.

visual.label: between two grains of sand
visual.sub: that's how far apart stars are

segments.text: What does collide is gas. Giant clouds smash together and squeeze into thousands of new stars.
segments.headline: Bursts of new stars

segments.text: Gravity pulls out long tails of stars, like in the Mice galaxies.
segments.headline: Long tails of stars

segments.text: The giant black holes at their centers sink together, and finally merge, shaking space with gravitational waves.
segments.headline: Black holes merge

segments.text: Our own Milky Way grew by swallowing smaller galaxies. About ten billion years ago, it ate one called Gaia-Enceladus.
segments.headline: The Milky Way eats galaxies

segments.text: And it's still eating. Smaller galaxies around us are being slowly torn apart right now.
segments.headline: Still eating

segments.text: Tomorrow, two galaxies you can see without a telescope, if you go south. And one day, we'll swallow them too. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
